behavior_items: The test defines a class `X` with a user-provided copy constructor `X(const X&) {}` and no default constructor shown. This makes initialization of `X` objects semantically important, because creating an element from `x` must go through copy construction rather than trivial initialization.

`extern X x;` declares a non-local source object whose value is not a constant expression. That matters because the array-new initializer cannot be folded as compile-time constant data; the front end must build runtime initialization logic.

The statement `new X[1]{x};` performs dynamic allocation of an array of one `X` and uses a braced initializer list to initialize the single element from `x`. In C++ terms, the allocated object is an array, and element 0 is copy-initialized/direct-list-initialized from the lvalue `x` via `X(const X&)`.

Because the initializer is non-constant and the destination is an array-new expression, the compiler must synthesize runtime construction code for array elements after allocation, rather than merely emitting a static initializer blob.

The reproducer specifically depends on `-std=c++14`. The bug report says the ICE happens in C++14 mode; this indicates the affected lowering path is sensitive to language-version-specific handling of array new with braced initialization and temporary/materialization rules in the C++ front end.

The reproducer also specifically depends on `-fno-elide-constructors`. Disabling constructor elision forces GCC to preserve explicit copy-construction behavior in the front-end tree representation instead of optimizing away certain intermediate construction steps. That changes the shape of the internal expression tree fed into gimplification.

The commented-out `constexpr` on the copy constructor is a clue that constant-evaluation properties affect whether GCC takes a constant-initializer path or a runtime-construction path. With the constructor non-`constexpr` and the source object external/non-constant, GCC must use the runtime path that triggers the bug.

The failure is not a user-visible semantic diagnostic; it is an internal compiler error. That means GCC accepts the source as valid C++ but crashes while lowering it to GIMPLE, specifically in C++-specific gimplification (`cp_gimplify_expr`) before normal code generation completes.

The backtrace shows the crash originates in `cp/cp-gimplify.cc:904` inside `cp_gimplify_expr`, and is reached during generic `gimplify_expr`, including `gimplify_addr_expr`, `gimplify_arg`, and `gimplify_call_expr`. This strongly suggests the front end produced a C++-specific tree node in or around the constructor/initializer sequence that generic gimplification expected to have been rewritten into a simpler form, but was not.

The appearance of `gimplify_addr_expr` in the stack is consistent with GCC taking the address of a constructed temporary or array element as part of lowering constructor calls for the array-new initialization. The ICE implies that one operand in this address-taking/constructor-call path remains in an unsupported C++ front-end form.

Because the crash requires both array new and a non-constant initializer, the exercised path is narrower than ordinary copy construction. A plain local variable initialization like `X y{x};` would use different lowering; here GCC must combine allocation, element-wise construction, cleanup handling for partially constructed arrays, and constructor-call sequencing.

The backtrace also includes cleanup/compound-expression gimplification (`gimplify_cleanup_point_expr`, `gimplify_compound_expr`), which matches the need to model exception-safe array construction: allocate storage, construct element(s), and arrange destruction/deallocation if construction throws. The buggy tree likely appears inside that compound/cleanup wrapper.

The bug is reported as a regression beginning with commit `6ffbf87ca66f4ed9cd79cff675fabe2109e46e85`, so the reproducer exercises code introduced or altered by that change. The report title mentions 'for non-constant initializer in array new', which aligns exactly with the runtime array-element initialization path triggered by `x`.

Semantically, a correct compiler should generate code equivalent to: allocate storage for one `X`, then invoke `X`'s copy constructor on the first array element using `x` as the source, and finally yield the pointer result of `new`. No diagnostic should be emitted, and certainly no ICE should occur.

In short, the reproducer stresses GCC's C++ front-end lowering of `new T[n]{init...}` when `T` has a non-trivial copy constructor, the initializer is runtime-only, and copy-elision is disabled. The compiler mishandles that internal representation during gimplification and crashes instead of producing normal code.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer is a valid C++14 program that dynamically allocates an array of one `X` and initializes the single element from an external object `x` using `X`'s copy constructor. Because `x` is non-constant and constructor elision is disabled, GCC must preserve explicit runtime copy-construction logic for the array-new initializer. In affected GCC versions, that combination leaves a C++-specific expression node in the array-construction lowering path, and `cp_gimplify_expr` crashes while converting the front-end tree to GIMPLE. The bug therefore exercises the runtime, exception-aware array-new initialization path for a non-trivially copy-constructed element under `-std=c++14 -fno-elide-constructors`, exposing a regression rather than any source-level language error.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The failure pattern is a front-end lowering regression in GCC's C++ path for array new with braced initialization when the initializer is runtime-only and copy construction cannot be elided. The key common traits are: valid C++14 source, dynamic array allocation (`new X[1]{x}`), non-trivial copy construction (`X(const X&)`), non-constant source object (`extern X x`), and dependence on `-fno-elide-constructors`. Together these force GCC to build explicit runtime element-construction trees, plus cleanup logic for array construction. The ICE occurs in `cp_gimplify_expr` during C++-specific gimplification, with the stack passing through address-of, call-argument, compound-expression, and cleanup-point lowering. This strongly indicates that the front end leaves behind an unsupported or unlowered C++ tree node in the array-new initialization sequence, likely related to temporary/materialization or constructor-call wrapping introduced by the regressing commit. Since the bug is specific to non-constant initializers and to disabled copy elision, the most plausible defects are in the runtime array-initializer expansion path rather than parsing, semantic checking, or the reproducer.

Create a brand new ..._TYPE node (which will be just a variant of the existing ..._TYPE node with identical properties) and then install X as the TYPE_NAME of this brand new (duplicate) ..._TYPE node. The whole point here is to end up with a situation where each and every ..._TYPE node the compiler creates will be uniquely associated with AT MOST one node representing a typedef name. This way, even though the compiler substitutes corresponding ..._TYPE nodes for TYPE_DECL (i.e. "typedef name") nodes very early on, later parts of the compiler can always do the reverse translation and get back the corresponding typedef name.
